n: In this lecture we begin the introduction to toxicological chemistry. The plan is as follows: the aim of the science, its link with other sciences, objects and methods of analysis, preliminary examination of the object, and forensic chemical examination. Key words: toxicology, toxicokinetics, toxicodynamics, forensic chemical examination, expert chemists and the report. This is a core module of the pharmaceutical profession; it teaches the isolation of poisonous and potent substances and the determination of their quality and quantity.

The word toxicology comes from the Greek toxikon, that is, poison, and logos, that is, I study. This science studies the action of poisons on the living organism. The action of a poison is studied in two directions. Toxicodynamics explains how a poison acts on the organism. Toxicokinetics shows what changes the poison undergoes in the organism. Do not confuse these two concepts.

At present there are three main directions in toxicology. The first is theoretical, that is, experimental toxicology: it studies the interaction of poison and organism. The second is preventive, that is, hygienic toxicology: it studies degrees of hazard and protection from them. The third is clinical toxicology. This is a medical science that studies chemical diseases arising from toxic action.

Clinical toxicology consists of four parts. The first is acute poisoning: it studies conditions arising from the action of chemical compounds in a high amount at one time. The second is continuous poisoning: it occurs when poisonous compounds act for a long time in small amounts. The third is narcological toxicology. It studies people's addiction to narcotic, that is, intoxicating, substances and measures to combat it. The fourth is toxicology of drug substances: it studies the side effects and toxic effects of medicinal substances.

t: The toxic situation and the scale of poisoning
n: Now about the toxic situation. The use of synthetic poisonous compounds in industry, agriculture, medicine and daily life creates an ecological hazard called the “toxic situation”. The number of poisonous compounds causing the most poisonings is over 500. Domestic poisoning, knowing or unknowing, makes up 98% of all poisonings. Occupational poisonings are mainly chronic. The main task of clinical toxicology: making the diagnosis, treatment and organising the prevention of poisoning.

Let us divide the factors influencing poisoning into groups. The main factors concerning the poison: physicochemical state, dose and concentration, distribution in the body, and chemical purity. Additional factors: speed and routes of entry, cumulation, combined action with other substances. On the part of the organism, the weight, nutrition, sex, age and general health of the victim are important. Predisposition is also important: allergy and tendency to toxicomania.

t: Causes influencing poisoning: main and additional
n: The causes of poisoning are divided into two groups. The first group is main causes: physicochemical state, dose and concentration, distribution in the body, chemical purity and foreign substances. The second group is additional causes: speed and routes of entry, cumulation or habituation to the poison, that is, privikanie, combined action with another drug. Also taken into account are visual and taste sensitivity, weight and manner of eating, sex, age, predisposition to allergy or toxicomania, and general health.

Chemical structure influences toxicity. Normal chain bonds of hydrocarbons are more toxic than their isomers. Cyclic compounds act more strongly than acyclic ones; for example, cyclopropane is stronger than propane. Halogen, nitro- and nitrosoamine groups and a double bond increase toxicity. The hydroxyl group, however, reduces it: an alcohol is less toxic than the hydrocarbon. For example, amyl alcohol is more toxic than propyl alcohol.

According to Richardson's rule, toxicity also increases with a rising homologous series and molecular mass. There is an exception to this rule: the first members of a homologous series are stronger poisons than the later ones. Examples: formic acid HCOOH is stronger than acetic acid CH3COOH. Formaldehyde CH2O is stronger than acetaldehyde. Methyl alcohol CH3OH is a stronger poison than ethyl alcohol C2H5OH.

t: Combined action, sex, age and prolonged exposure
n: Poisoning may occur with several poisons. Changes in the environment, such as high temperature, also act in combination. Sensitivity differs by sex: men are sensitive to organophosphorus substances, nicotine and insulin, whereas women are hypersensitive to carbon monoxide, morphine and barbiturates. Sensitivity to a poison varies with age: one group of poisons acts strongly on the young, others on the elderly. Prolonged exposure leads to conditions such as idiosyncrasy, allergy, dependence, toxicomania, alcoholism, morphinism and cocainism.

What does toxicological chemistry study? The module isolates poisonous substances and their transformation products from tissues, organs, fluids and the environment by chemical methods and determines their quality and quantity. The media examined: biological objects and the environment, that is, water, soil, air, food remnants and drugs. The main aim is to study methods of isolating and identifying poisonous compounds and their breakdown products from a biological object. Everyone who has acquired the specialty of pharmacist must be able to work in the roles of forensic chemical expert and chemist-toxicologist.

t: Aim of teaching and three sections
n: The aim of the module is to identify poisonous drug substances and breakdown products in biological fluids and tissues. In addition, students are taught to perform laboratory rapid analytical methods for detecting signs of poisoning. Toxicological chemistry consists of three sections. The first is forensic chemistry, the most fundamental and most complex section. The second is the national-economy section: identification from biological objects. The third is express analysis: rapid analysis in acute poisoning.

Let us consider the link with other sciences. The module is among the pharmaceutical modules and is taught at pharmaceutical faculties. Pharmacology and toxicology give the action of a poison on organs. Analytical and organic chemistry serve the determination of quality and quantity. In the study of metabolites it is linked with toxicological, biological, analytical and pharmaceutical chemistry. Because the cause of poisoning is often a plant, the chemist must know pharmacognosy.

The objects of chemical-toxicological analysis are divided into three groups. The first is objects taken from the body: organs, blood, urine and vomit. The second is products and environment: food, water, drugs and air. The third is articles: clothing, stains and drug containers. In a survivor, gastric lavage fluid, vomit, blood and urine are taken; the general name is “biological object”. The air of an industrial enterprise and of a home is also an object if it is the source of poisoning.

The rules for preserving a biological object are as follows. On hot days, if the object is to be sent far away, ethyl alcohol is used as the preservative. If it is recommended that the object be examined for ethyl alcohol and nitrite, preservation with ethyl alcohol is prohibited. Together with the preserved object, a sample of the ethyl alcohol must also be sent to the laboratory. Remember: this requirement is needed for correct assessment of the analytical result.

t: Dispatch of the object and the label
n: The procedure for dispatching the object is carried out in sequence. First the jar is closed tightly. Then a lead seal is applied. Then the label is written. The label states the name of the deceased, year of birth, name of the organ, the examination report and the serial number of the jar. Then the referral or order is attached: with the bio-object, the expert's referral or the order of the investigating bodies for examination is sent. Finally the object is sent to the laboratory.

There are six distinctive features of the examination. Poisons are varied, that is, from different groups of chemical compounds. Objects are also varied, and a small amount of poison is isolated from many bio-objects. One does not work with a pure substance but with an extract containing foreign substances. The isolated poison is present in extremely small amounts. Because the poison is altered in the body, altered products, that is, metabolites, are also determined. And finally, the forensic chemist is answerable to the judicial and investigating bodies.

Methods of analysis are divided into two groups: isolation and purification, and determination of the quality and quantity of the isolated substance. The chain of analysis is as follows: isolation from the object, purification of the extract, determination of quality, determination of quantity. The result of isolation is a liquid in the form of distillate, mineralisate or dialysate. The method depends on the type of object: isolating an alkaloid from an organ differs from isolating it from urine.

We put the methods of isolation and purification in a table. In isolation, steam distillation, decomposition, maceration with solvents and dialysis are used. In purification, extraction, chromatographic methods, dry distillation, microdiffusion and the like are used. That is, isolation extracts the substance from the object, whereas purification frees it from foreign admixtures.

t: Stages of isolation and purification: general scheme
n: Isolation of substances from a biological object is carried out in two stages. The first is isolation in the form of distillate, mineralisate or dialysate. The second is purification. The isolated and purified substance is identified by chemical, microchemical and microcrystalloscopic methods, TLC, spectral and pharmacological methods. General order: isolation from the object, purification, determination of quality, determination of quantity.

t: Methods of identification and quantitative methods
n: Let us consider the methods of identification. For qualitative identification, chemical, microchemical and microcrystalloscopic methods, thin-layer chromatography, that is, TLC, spectral characterisation and pharmacological action are used. For quantitative determination, acidimetry, alkalimetry, complexometry, photometry, spectrophotometry, extraction photometry or the gas chromatographic method is used. In preliminary orienting examination, microdiffusion, microcrystalloscopic reactions and chromatographic “screening” are mainly used.

t: Preliminary examination and the examination plan
n: On the preliminary examination and the examination plan. Because testing for each poison takes much time, the forensic chemist draws up a clear plan. The bases of the plan: the referral from the judicial body, the case history, the forensic medical examination report, the pH, odour and colour of the object, and preliminary orienting results. If the orienting examination is positive, the main examination for the suspected substance must be carried out. Physical evidence is often an object that cannot be replaced, so caution and economy are required.

On the methods of preliminary examination. Some orienting methods are highly sensitive but not specific. They are often used in express examination. Because of sensitivity, a reaction may detect even a substance in a therapeutic dose. Therefore additional analysis is carried out. In old referrals, for white arsenic, porcelain-like fragments, the Reinsch method, that is, Hg and As, the Gutzeit method, and tests for hydrocyanic acid and nitrite are given.

Preliminary examination by external signs is as follows. A foreign inclusion, for example crystals of arsenic oxide or plant seeds, is picked out with forceps. Odour is well perceived in an unputrefied object. Products of putrefaction alter the odour of poisons. A bitter almond odour points to cyanides. The odour of pyridine bases indicates denatured alcohol. Yellow colour points to picric acid, strychnine or chromates. Black colour indicates sulphuric acid.

Determining pH is part of the preliminary examination. If the pH is 3 or less, mineral acids are mainly present, or organic acids in large amounts. A weakly acid medium in putrefied organs often indicates a fermentation process. An alkaline medium gives a pointer to test the object for alkalis or carbonates. pH ranges of indicators: litmus 5.0-8.0, Congo red 3.0-5.2, phenolphthalein 8.2-10.0.

The analysis of the expert chemist may be directed or undirected. Directed analysis is carried out for one or several substances on the instruction of forensic medical or investigating staff. In undirected, that is, general, analysis, testing is for the 67 poisonous and potent substances included in the ministry's order. Incomplete analysis is carried out for one or several substances on separate instruction. In complete analysis the expert must test for 67 substances.

Let us consider the groups of the 67 substances. 13 volatile poisons: hydrocyanic acid, alcohols, formaldehyde, chloroform, chloral hydrate, dichloroethane and phenols. 13 metal salts: barium, manganese, chromium, zinc, thallium, lead, copper, mercury and others. By the acidified water and alcohol method, 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 synthetic substances are isolated. Substances isolated with an organic solvent include, for example, carbophos, metaphos, chlorophos and sevin.

Poisons are divided into groups according to the methods of isolation from the object. The first group is volatile poisons: they are distilled with steam. Examples: cyanide and acetic acid, halogen compounds, alcohol, aldehyde and phenols. The second group is isolated by extraction with an acidified polar solvent: barbiturates and alkaloids. The third group is metal poisons, isolated by mineralisation: heavy metals and arsenic.

The fourth group of poisons is the dialysis group: maceration with water and dialysis, for example mineral acids and alkalis. The fifth group is isolated by maceration with an organic solvent: pesticides and cardiac glycosides. The sixth group is isolated by special, specific methods: TEL, zinc phosphide and fluorides. Chloral hydrate and phenol are isolated both by steam and by acidified water and alcohol. Chlorophos is isolated by steam distillation, acidified water and alcohol, and ether maceration. The results of the methods are compared, and the method by which most substance was isolated is chosen.

t: Six groups of poisons by method of isolation
n: Poisons are divided into six groups according to the method of isolation from the object. The first is volatile poisons, distilled with steam. The second is isolated with acidified water and alcohol. The third is isolated by mineralisation. The fourth is isolated by maceration with water or by dialysis. The fifth is by maceration with an organic solvent, and the sixth by special methods, that is, TEL, zinc phosphide and fluorides.

t: Some substances are isolated by several methods
n: Some substances are isolated by several methods. Chloral hydrate and phenol, besides steam distillation, are also isolated with acidified water and alcohol, with an organic solvent, or by maceration with water. Liquid alkaloids are isolated with acidified water and alcohol, and also by distillation. Chlorophos is isolated by steam distillation, acidified water and alcohol, and ether maceration. The results of the methods are compared, and the method by which most substance was isolated is chosen.

Let us consider the methods of isolation. In extraction, a substance dissolved in water is extracted with an organic solvent immiscible with water; this is the main method for biological fluids. Steam distillation is used for poisons such as hydrocyanic acid, alcohols, formaldehyde, hexachloran and nicotine. Vacuum distillation is at low temperature and is used for substances that decompose at high heat, for example tetraethyl lead. Metal poisons are isolated by wet or dry mineralisation, that is, destruction, methods.

Extraction is based on the partition coefficient. K = C(organic solution) / C(water). For a substance soluble in an organic solvent, K is greater than one. The nature of the solvent, the pH of the medium and electrolytes strongly influence solubility. Substances with acidic properties dissolve well in water in an alkaline medium. Alkaloids, by contrast, dissolve well in an organic solvent in an alkaline medium and in water in an acid medium. Re-extraction is based on changing the pH of the aqueous solution.

Let us list the methods of purifying the extract. Saponification, for compounds resistant to hydrolysis: the fat is hydrolysed, then the main substance is extracted, for example organochlorine compounds. Re-extraction is based on changing the pH of the aqueous solution. Sulphonation is used for substances resistant to sulphuric acid in a fat-rich extract, for example for barbiturates. Chromatography is of thin-layer and gas-liquid types. Fats and waxy substances, on cooling in acetone to -70 °C, float up and are separated.

On orienting examination and screening. The Radionova method separates 49 drug substances by TLC “screening”; it is also used in poisoning of children. Kartoshov proposed distinguishing 83 nitrogen-containing poisons by TLC screening on the basis of 5 standard substances. The TLC screening of the department's staff makes it possible to identify and distinguish organophosphorus compounds. Orienting tests in urine: cobalt acetate with NH3 or Li alkali shows barbiturates, and ferric chloride and sulphuric acid show phenothiazines with a pale red colour.

Biotransformation and metabolites. Metabolism, from the Greek metabol, that is, change, is the conversion of a substance from one chemical structure to another. A poison or drug is metabolically altered regardless of the route by which it entered the body. This is expressed by the term biotransformation. The altered products of substances are called metabolites; they are sometimes hyperactive, but more often have reduced or lost activity. Substances foreign to the organism are called xenobiotics: xenos foreign, bios life.

Metabolic change is a means of defence, but sometimes a more poisonous metabolite is formed; this is called lethal synthesis. Types of reaction: oxidation, reduction, dealkylation, deamination, hydrolysis and conjugation. Examples: in oxidation the phenyl of phenobarbital passes to hydroxyphenyl. In reduction chloral hydrate is converted to trichloroethanol. In dealkylation prominal passes to phenobarbital. In hydrolysis heroin, with two molecules of water, breaks down into morphine and acetic acid. Conjugation is combination with endogenous compounds, that is, glucuronic and sulphuric acid: phenol is converted to phenyl sulphate.

Poisoning is classified by origin, by how it arises, and by clinical features. By origin it is accidental or intentional, and intentional is divided into suicidal and criminal types. By occurrence, industrial, domestic and medical poisoning are distinguished. The route of entry is peroral, inhalational or injectional. By clinical features there are acute and chronic poisoning. In acute poisoning a large amount enters at once; in chronic, a small amount enters over a long time in portions. The nosological classification is linked with the name of the chemical compound.

t: Assessing the result: why a substance may not be found
n: In assessing the result, one must know why a substance may not be found. The substance may have been eliminated from the body before death, have undergone metabolic change, or have broken down altogether. It may also not be found because it combined with other substances or because the sensitivity of the method of detection is low. When a substance is found, quantitative analysis is mandatory. In some cases reactions characteristic of a harmless substance may also appear: the substance was taken as a medicine, metals always present in the object, products of putrefaction, or a substance added from the external environment.

t: Retention periods for physical evidence and documents
n: The retention periods for physical evidence and documents are as follows. If the object is preserved, it is kept for up to 1 year. Documents are kept in a safe and discarded after 1 year. Objects containing alcohol are discarded after 1 month.

t: Centres for treatment of acute poisoning
n: The second part of toxicological chemistry is express analysis of objects in centres for the treatment of acute poisoning. The first toxicological team was organised in 1961 at the hospital of the Moscow ambulance station; it had no post of chemist. In 1963 a centre was opened at the Sklifosovsky Institute, and in 1964 at the Filatov Children's Hospital. By Ministry of Health order No. 475 of 6 May 1980, departments for the treatment of acute poisoning began work in all republican and regional centres. From 1987 narcological laboratories were organised.

Let us conclude. Toxicological chemistry teaches the isolation of poisonous substances from a biological object and the determination of their quality and quantity. Order of work: preliminary examination and plan, isolation, purification, determination of quality and quantity. By method of isolation, poisons are divided into 6 groups: volatile, acidified, mineralisation, dialysis, organic solvent and special methods. For self-check ask yourself: what are the groups of objects, what is the preservation rule, what are the methods of isolation and purification, what is the significance of pH?
